catalog_quote: 1.3.1 The phonological word (with a few exceptions) has at least one high tone, if we assume that falling = HI/LO, rising = LO/HI, and glottal = HI'. Evidence for this analysis lies in the fact that FA and RI occur only on long vowels (though there are problems with this; see below and IV.D). The phonological word is defined on the basis of tones, syllable structure, and co-occurrence restrictions. Thus postpositions (KPOS) are considered clitics, as are some forms of the auxiliary (KAUX). 1.3.2 Tones and Suprasegmentals. Laguna is a pitch-accent language, and there are five "phonetic" tones: low, high, falling, rising, glottal (LO, HI, FA, RI, GL). [p. 20] ... at this point I would analyze tone as a melody overlaying the word, partly conditioned by length. Some problems are discussed in IV.D. Tone also can be "morphemic", marking the difference between different forms of verbs; cf. V.D for examples. I assume that tone is placed on inflected words at the level of stem, and theme, with further tone change conditioned by vowel-final pronominal prefixes, number prefixes, and some suffixes. [p. 24] ... I begin with the following "strong" hypothesis for all Keresan: Keresan is a pitch accent language, using only high and low tones; the melody is high/low for most of the dialects, but not for Laguna or Acoma. [pp. 481-482] ... There is no word larger than one syllable without tones (except kum'e 'or'). [p. 488]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Laguna (Western) Keres has a lexical tonal (pitch) accent, not positional stress: each phonological word carries at least one HI tone (falling, rising and glottal 'tones' analysed as HI-containing contours, LO as residual), and where the HI tones fall is determined lexically and by morphology (stem/theme tone melodies altered by pronominal and number prefixes and some suffixes), so accent position is not predictable from syllable count or weight. Distributional limits: no long vowel occurs before the first HI of a word; falling tone occurs only on a long vowel before a short voiced low vowel and is always the last tone of the word; only low-toned vowels devoice. No rule of word stress is given; the author remarks only that 'the possibility of a combination of stress and tone should not be ignored' (p. ~492).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. (Spencer 1940, superseded, speaks of a secondary accent 'usually on the ultima' in polysyllables.)
new_statements.exceptions: A few toneless words (e.g. kum'e 'or'); postpositions and some auxiliary forms are toneless clitics; 'positive low' tone needed word-finally in certain lexical classes to block devoicing; Spanish loanwords commonly show falling-low melody; free variation between rising tone, V'V and glottal tone in some words (e.g. 'earth').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including clitics (postpositions, some auxiliaries); citation/phrase-final forms add echo vowels after glottal tone and extra sonorant glottalization in slow speech; downdrift across words noted for Acoma (Miller, via Valiquette). Statement is for the Laguna dialect; author extends the pitch accent characterisation to Acoma and all Keresan ('all seem to be pitch accent systems', p. 17).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Laguna dialect of Western Keres (Valiquette's fieldwork at Laguna Pueblo); Acoma, the other Western Keres dialect, is described first-hand by Miller 1965 and Maring 1967 (not accessible here) and second-hand as having the same type of system (tonal accents high/falling/glottal per Miller; four tones per Maring). Spencer 1940 is pan-Keresan with 'southern' (Acoma-Laguna) and 'northern' (Rio Grande = Eastern Keres, east2570) data mixed, and its stress-only analysis is superseded. Davis 1964/1989 material cited concerns Santa Ana, Santo Domingo and Cochiti (Eastern Keres, east2570), where Valiquette and Davis report a simpler, mostly word-initial HI accent -- that pattern should not be attributed to west2632.

sources.note: Laguna is a pitch accent (tone) language: HI vs residual LO plus falling, rising, glottal contours; every phonological word has at least one HI; tone is lexical and morphological (placed at stem/theme level, shifted by prefixes/suffixes); distributional constraints (no long vowel before first HI; falling tone only on a long vowel before a short voiced low vowel, always the last tone); no positional stress rule; notes in passing that stress may co-occur with tone (p.~481, ~492) and that Strauss & Furch analysed Acoma tonal accent, stress and devoicing via the foot.

sources.citation: Spencer, Robert Francis. 1940. A Preliminary Sketch of Keresan Grammar. M.A. thesis, University of New Mexico. xvi+170 pp. (UNM Digital Repository anth_etds/134, open access)
sources.note: Pan-Keresan ('southern' dialect = Acoma, Laguna; 'northern' = Rio Grande pueblos). pp. 20-21 'Accent': no rule covers every case; stress is 'recessive', trisyllables tend to antepenult, disyllables vary, polysyllables initial or second syllable with secondary accent usually on the ultima; nouns/adjectives generally penult, verbs initial; 'There are no tones in Keresan' (p. 21) -- a pre-phonemic analysis contradicted by all later work (Miller 1965, Davis 1964, Valiquette 1990), which treat Keresan accent as tonal.
